prompt: What is the main reason to read a project's full contribution guide (not just skim the root CONTRIBUTING.md) before opening your first PR?
choices: It usually contains project-specific mechanical requirements — like DCO sign-off, changelog file format, or local dev setup — that will get your PR bounced if ignored
It is legally required before you can submit any open-source contribution
It guarantees a maintainer will merge your PR without review
It replaces the need to read any of the actual source code

prompt: Which signal most reliably indicates a GitHub issue is a tractable first contribution, beyond just carrying a 'good first issue' label?
choices: It has the largest number of comments and community engagement
It has been open the longest, proving maintainers consider it low priority
It is scoped to a single subsystem, is reproducible quickly, and a maintainer has already confirmed an approach in the comments
It is labeled 'help wanted' regardless of how many files or subsystems it touches

prompt: In terraform-provider-aws's codebase structure, where would you look first to find the implementation of the `aws_instance` resource?
choices: internal/service/ec2/instance.go
The root main.go file
website/docs/r/instance.html.markdown
The terraform-plugin-sdk repository itself, since providers don't implement resources directly

prompt: What do the Create/Read/Update/Delete functions in a Terraform provider resource file actually do?
choices: They are unused legacy scaffolding kept for backward compatibility
They translate Terraform's desired-state lifecycle operations into calls against the underlying cloud provider's SDK, and write results back into Terraform state
They only run during `terraform plan`, never during `terraform apply`
They directly edit the .tf configuration files on disk

prompt: Why does terraform-provider-aws require a separate file per PR under .changelog/ instead of a hand-edited CHANGELOG.md?
choices: Because the changelog is auto-deleted after each release and needs to be rebuilt
To avoid merge conflicts from hundreds of concurrent PRs all editing the same shared file, and to let CI validate each entry's format automatically
Because CHANGELOG.md is reserved for security advisories only
It is purely a stylistic preference with no functional purpose

prompt: How does the Kubernetes Enhancement Proposal (KEP) process most fundamentally differ from how terraform-provider-aws typically handles a new feature proposal?
choices: KEPs require SIG sponsorship and a staged, milestone-gated written design doc with a Production Readiness Review, while most terraform-provider-aws changes are approved through informal GitHub issue discussion and a maintainer comment
Both projects require an identical formal RFC document before any code can be written
Terraform-provider-aws requires more governance sign-offs than Kubernetes because it has more active contributors
KEPs are optional design notes with no bearing on whether code actually merges

prompt: A KEP's kep.yaml lists `stage: alpha`. What does that indicate about the feature?
choices: The feature has no code yet and is still just an idea under discussion
The feature is fully stable, on by default, and covered by Kubernetes' API compatibility guarantees
The feature is implemented behind a feature gate, off by default, and not yet guaranteed to be API-stable
The feature has been rejected and will not be implemented

prompt: You already know from Tier 3 that a Deployment reconciles desired vs. actual pod state through a controller loop. How does that same pattern help you orient in cert-manager's codebase?
choices: It doesn't apply — cert-manager uses a completely unrelated architecture with no controllers
It means cert-manager's Certificate and Issuer CRDs are reconciled by controller packages, so the real logic lives in the reconcilers, not in the CRD schema definitions
It means you should only read the CRD YAML schemas, since the controllers are auto-generated and contain no custom logic
It means cert-manager requires its own separate Kubernetes cluster that doesn't use controllers at all
